title: The moments and asymptotic spectral distribution of the Grassmannian ensemble
summary: In this paper, we study random density matrices constructed by taking partial traces of projections onto random subspaces of a bipartite Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_{B}$ distributed according to the pushforward measure of the action of the unitary group on the Grassmannian $\text{Gr}_{n}(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_{B})$. This ensemble models a `typical' quantum subspace. All tracial moments of the density operator, as well as mixed tracial moments of reduced density operators, are computed explicitly using Weingarten calculus. There are several consequences of these results. In particular, we prove that the empirical spectral distribution of the density operator converges almost surely to a rescaled Marchenko-Pastur law. We also prove that this ensemble can be written as a sum of asymptotically free random density operators, leading to an alternative proof of the convergence of the spectral distribution. Finally, we compute the asymptotic expansion of the average entanglement entropy.

title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables. Code, data and scripts to reproduce all experiments: https://github.com/anapaulaappel/QPUScheduler
summary: Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.

title: A Microwave-Photonics Formulation of the Rydberg-Atom Receiver
summary: The performance of Rydberg-atom receivers is seldom stated as a radio-frequency (RF) link budget. The receiver is shown to be an intensity-modulated direct-detection analog optical link whose modulator is the laser-driven vapor. The transmission of a warm vapor is derived in closed form by averaging the four-level response over atomic velocities. The conversion gain, noise figure, bandwidth, intercept points, and spurious-free dynamic range follow from this one function. For a weak probe the instantaneous bandwidth is half the width of the transparency window in two-photon detuning. The local-oscillator beat places the second-order intercept near twice the local-oscillator field, so the local oscillator sets the even-order linearity. For a rubidium transition at 17.04 GHz the closed forms agree with a velocity-resolved density-matrix model to 1% for the slope and the intercepts and to 10% for the bandwidth. They underestimate the group delay by a third. The response is tied to atomic constants, and the sensing volume escapes the Chu limit. However, the noise figure of a warm vapor rules it out as a general replacement for an antenna and low-noise amplifier.

title: Nonperturbative Bounds on the Ground-State Energy of Lattice QED
summary: We establish nonperturbative bounds on the ground-state energy of lattice quantum electrodynamics with naive fermions in Coulomb gauge, within the Gaussian photon approximation. Our central result is a spectral comparison theorem showing that, in the thermodynamic limit, the minimum fermionic energy density over all link configurations coincides with that of the trivial gauge configuration. The proof exploits a logarithmic determinant representation and dimensional reduction, without relying on reflection positivity, and applies to lattices of either parity. Combining this result with the positivity of the electromagnetic and Coulomb Hamiltonians, we derive an explicit lower bound on the interacting ground-state energy. Finite-lattice counterexamples show that the thermodynamic limit is essential.

title: Topological phases protected by half-chiral symmetry
summary: Chiral (or sublattice) symmetry describes bipartite systems such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain where same-sublattice A-A and B-B hoppings are forbidden, enabling the protection of topological phases. Here we identify new topological phases protected by half-chiral symmetry wherein chiral symmetry is preserved on only one sublattice, as may occur with sublattice imbalance (e.g. graphene-hBN) or localized orbitals (e.g. zincblende). Unlike conventional symmetry operators described by group theory, half-chiral symmetry is an algebraic constraint on the sublattice-projected Hamiltonian such as $PHP=0$, requiring a new framework for topological protection. We develop such a framework, identifying real-space bulk topological invariants and corresponding topological boundary modes that stick to zero energy. In two dimensions we construct a half-chiral Kekule honeycomb model and show that its unusual higher-order topology protects a single zero-energy mode at a single corner.

title: Quantum-Chaos-Assisted Measure Synchronization in a Double-Well Ultracold Bose Gas
summary: This paper investigates measure synchronization (MS) in a two-component ultracold atomic system confined in a double-well potential, which realizes a quantum many-body bosonic Josephson junction. Through spectral-statistics analysis, we identify the quantum chaotic parameter regime and confirm that the system achieves MS within this regime with weak dependence on the initial energy imbalance. We further show that chaotic dynamics not only significantly shortens the time scale for establishing synchronization but is also accompanied by entanglement entropy approaching the random-state prediction. These results reveal close connections among quantum chaos, MS, and quantum entanglement in conservative quantum many-body systems and may motivate further studies on the underlying mechanisms of chaos-assisted synchronization.

title: Bayesian Quantum Thermometry of Ultracold Gases with Non-Equilibrium Single-Atom Probes
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures. The data that support the findings of this study are openly available at the following URL/DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24390998
summary: Precise thermometry is essential for experiments with ultracold quantum gases, but conventional techniques such as time-of-flight thermometry are destructive and lose sensitivity at low atomic densities. Quantum probes provide an alternative route by encoding temperature information in accessible internal degrees of freedom. Here, we implement Bayesian thermometry with non-equilibrium spin-based single-atom probes immersed in an ultracold atomic bath. Temperature-dependent spin-exchange collisions map the bath temperature onto the internal spin populations of the probe atoms. Measurements of these populations are then used to iteratively update a Bayesian temperature estimate. We connect the information gained at different measurement settings to the underlying spin dynamics, identifying intersections of temperature-dependent population trajectories as a source of thermometric ambiguity. Using the expected information gain to optimize measurement settings, we experimentally compare unoptimized, a priori optimized, and adaptively optimized protocols. Both optimized protocols accelerate convergence, with the adaptive protocol reducing the average number of measurements required to reach a prescribed precision by a factor of 2.5 compared with the unoptimized protocol. In the many-measurement regime, we further characterize the protocols through their asymptotic error scaling and the accumulation of Fisher information, while testing consistency with the expected Cramér-Rao bound (ECRB) and the Bernstein-von Mises theorem. These results connect the microscopic dynamics of a quantum probe to efficient measurement design and establish Bayesian spin thermometry as a practical approach for ultracold-gas experiments.

title: Pseudo-entropy in Thouless Pumps and Majorana Topological Phases
summary: We study the average excess pseudo entropy, $ΔS_{12}$, in the Rice-Mele model under Thouless pumping. We compute it for two driving schemes, the control-freak and smooth pumps, under open and periodic boundary conditions. We find that $ΔS_{12}$ distinguishes the trivial, monomer, and topological stages of the pump, and that it depends on the boundary condition, the driving scheme, and the reference time. We also find that a nonzero staggered potential breaks chiral symmetry and gaps out the SSH critical point, thereby flattening the pseudo-entropy peak at the phase boundary. We also study reference-state dependence in the open Kitaev chain, comparing a fixed even-parity target with five reference families: even free-fermion, pairing-only, vacuum, and two fixed gapped states. We find that the pseudo-entropy response depends on the reference and on the parity of the subsystem size, even when the reference remains gapped. At $μ=0$, the pairing-only reference gives the exact result $S_{\mathrm{pr}}=\ln 2$ for $L=4m+2$, while the $L=4m$ sequence has analytically determined finite-size corrections. These results show that, in both models, pseudo entropy is a property of the reference-target pair and the subsystem partition, rather than a reference-independent signature of the topological phase.

title: Thermo-electric Response Bound on Fluctuations in Coherent Transport
summary: We establish an accessible lower bound on current noise in coherent electron transport, expressed in terms of responses to reservoir temperatures and chemical potentials. Derived within the Floquet-Nambu scattering formalism using a Cramér-Rao-type inequality, it holds for arbitrary linear combinations of charge and heat currents in normal terminals, including those of hybrid superconducting systems, under static or periodic driving. The bound is tight in experimentally relevant regimes, notably in quantum point contacts with static or oscillating voltages and normal-superconductor junctions, often providing stronger constraints than thermodynamic uncertainty relations. It can be evaluated via experimentally accessible response coefficients, without inferring entropy production or dynamical activity, and provides useful constraints on the precision of nanoscale thermal and quantum devices.

title: Quantum Many-Body Scars from Operator Size
summary: We present a general construction of approximate many-body scar states in two copies of a system using a bilocal size interaction that couples one site to its partner on the other copy. For an uncoupled two-sided Hamiltonian whose terms have fixed size in an operator basis, we identify polynomially many Krylov basis states that it annihilates and that, in the thermodynamic limit, become concentrated on a single size sector. The size operator splits them into a tower of equally spaced levels that gives rise to coherent revivals characterized by collective oscillations of energy across the two copies. We provide a concrete realization of this construction in two copies of a general $q$-body nearest-neighbor spin chain, and the SYK model.
